input.question: The human bodies needs 20 amino acids, 10 are essential; are there other common animals or plants that use different amino acids? Is there a theoretical limit to the amount of amino acids possible?
input.ground_truth: Amino acids can be post-translationally be modified, so there is a large variety in that area. Also, the 21 (not 20) "standard" amino acids are commonly found in eukaryotes. Prokaryotes (bacteria and such) also have other amino acids like selocysteine and pyrrolysine.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: The human bodies needs 20 amino acids, 10 are essential; are there other common animals or plants that use different amino acids? Is there a theoretical limit to the amount of amino acids possible?

response.prediction:
Okay! Imagine your body is like a big LEGO set, and the LEGO bricks are like amino acids. Your body needs 20 special LEGO bricks (amino acids) to build everything it needs. Out of these 20, 10 are super special bricks that you can only get from your food—you can’t make them yourself, so you *have* to eat them.

Now, other animals and plants are also building their own LEGO sets, but sometimes they use different kinds of bricks! For example, some animals can make all the bricks they need by themselves, so they don’t have to eat as many special ones. Some plants use a little bit different set of bricks too.

As for the “theoretical limit”—that means, “how many different LEGO bricks could there ever be?” Scientists think there could be a lot, maybe even more than we know about! But most living things on Earth only use about 20 common ones. It’s kind of like how you can make lots of different things with your LEGO set, but you don’t need thousands of different shapes to build cool stuff.

So, different living things use different LEGO bricks (amino acids), and there could be many more kinds out there, but we mostly use about 20.
